source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

coverage.assignment: Full study pp. 670–676 and 683–690, INCLUDING presidential immunity pp. 683–685; skim pp. 676–683. Distinction reflected in separate topic.
coverage.syllabusUnit: VI.C — Availability and Timing of Judicial Review
coverage.sourceLimit: Canvas ACUS Recommendation 75-3 is assigned separately and not in this upload

topics.title: § 10.1.1 — Jurisdiction: Which Court Reviews? (pp. 670–673)
topics.description: Detailed assigned reading: statutory review routes, exclusivity, court-of-appeals versus trial court, federal-question review, sovereign immunity waiver.

entries.title: Two threshold requirements: jurisdiction and cause of action
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Plaintiff seeking judicial relief must establish a court's subject-matter jurisdiction and a recognized cause of action supporting the requested remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: You need the right courthouse AND a legal basis to ask it to help.
entries.legalExplanation: Jurisdiction identifies adjudicative authority; cause of action authorizes the claim and relief. The federal APA does not itself grant subject-matter jurisdiction.
entries.examApplication: Begin a reviewability essay by naming court, statutory jurisdiction, cause of action and remedy.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume that APA §§ 701–706 alone give federal courts jurisdiction.

entries.title: Specific statutory judicial review ordinarily exclusive
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: An agency's enabling act may designate reviewing court, eligibility to sue, timing and procedure; a prescribed review path is usually exclusive.
entries.laymanExplanation: If Congress directs appeals to one court within a deadline, you normally must use that route.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal trend directs review of final rules and orders to courts of appeals; state procedures usually begin in trial courts. Review statute controls rather than free court choice.
entries.examApplication: Read explicit review provision before turning to § 1331 or state general review law.
entries.examTrap: Do not attempt district-court § 1331 end-run around exclusive appellate statutory procedure.

entries.title: Federal rule/order review: appeal court preference
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: When statutory review allocation is ambiguous, courts may favor appellate review of agency rules and final orders unless new evidence needs to be received.
entries.laymanExplanation: Review is similar to an appeal; a panel can review a built record without conducting trial.
entries.legalExplanation: Citizens Awareness Network extended appellate review statute referencing 'orders' to NRC procedural rules; ACUS Recommendation 2024–1 recommends appellate forum for notice/comment rules.
entries.examApplication: Discuss importance, record completeness, volume of cases, and whether additional evidence necessary.
entries.examTrap: A recommendation or construction preference cannot override clear jurisdictional statute.

entries.title: Why trial courts sometimes preferable
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: High-volume low-stakes disability disputes may be handled more efficiently in district courts, while immigration appeals create major appellate workload.
entries.laymanExplanation: One judge closer to home may be cheaper than a three-judge appeals panel.
entries.legalExplanation: The source explores proposed specialized Social Security court and risks of agency capture versus specialized efficiency.

entries.title: State general review statute and New York Article 78
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: When no special review provision, state APA or general review law ordinarily channels agency challenges to designated trial court; New York Article 78 may transfer formal-adjudication disputes to appellate court.
entries.laymanExplanation: States offer a general way to challenge agencies even without a special appeal rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Select governing state procedural mechanism; do not assume federal route governs state agency.
entries.examApplication: Say what statutory review route applies in the hypothetical's state.
entries.examTrap: Federal § 1331 cannot be used to review purely state-law issues absent federal question.

entries.title: 28 U.S.C. § 1331 permits nonstatutory federal agency review
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Absent specific federal judicial review jurisdiction, a federal district court can hear federal-question challenges to agency and officer action through 28 U.S.C. § 1331.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a statute lacks a special appeal route, § 1331 usually opens a federal district courthouse for federal-law claims.
entries.legalExplanation: Apply federal-question jurisdiction, applicable APA rules, reviewability and sovereign immunity waiver separately.
entries.examApplication: Identify plaintiff's federal constitutional/statutory claim and § 1331 jurisdiction.
entries.examTrap: § 1331 does not automatically establish a claim for damages or remove all reviewability obstacles.

entries.title: APA § 702 waiver of sovereign immunity for nonmonetary relief
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Congress in 1976 waived federal sovereign immunity for actions seeking relief other than money damages against the United States, agency or official, subject to applicable limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can ordinarily sue an agency to stop unlawful action or obtain a declaration without suing only one officer as a workaround.
entries.legalExplanation: APA §§ 702–703 furnish waiver and forms of relief; § 1331 generally provides jurisdiction when specific review statute does not.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish injunction/declaration from money damages and identify proper federal defendant.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat § 702 as unrestricted waiver for tort damages or substitute for jurisdiction.

entries.title: APA § 703 forms of review and federal venue
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Section 703 permits agency review through special statutory proceedings or applicable legal action; § 1391(e) provides federal officer/agency venue by residence, cause, relevant property or (for no real property) plaintiff residence.
entries.laymanExplanation: The law tells you both which court has power and where to file it.
entries.legalExplanation: Proper defendant may be United States, agency by official title or official; APA § 703 and relevant federal civil rules govern.
entries.examApplication: After jurisdiction, briefly check venue, plaintiff/defendant, exclusivity and timing.
entries.examTrap: Venue is not the same as jurisdiction.

entries.title: Califano v. Sanders, 430 U.S. 99 (1977)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Federal APA provides review rules but not an independent grant of district-court jurisdiction.
entries.laymanExplanation: APA is a statute governing review, not the source of the court's subject-matter power.
entries.legalExplanation: Use § 1331 or specific judicial-review statute for jurisdiction.
entries.examApplication: In essays, separate APA cause/waiver from § 1331.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Citizens Awareness Network v. United States, 391 F.3d 338 (1st Cir. 2004)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Ambiguous NRC statutory appellate-review provision construed to reach procedural rules, not merely individual orders.
entries.laymanExplanation: When no new evidence required, appellate forum is apt.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory context and review function favored direct appellate route.
entries.examApplication: Compare trial v appellate review.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

topics.title: § 10.1.2 — Injunctions, Declaratory Relief and Writs (pp. 673–676)
topics.description: Detailed assigned reading: nonstatutory equitable relief; mandamus limits; certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto and habeas.

entries.title: APA § 703: injunction and declaratory judgment
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Without special review statute, plaintiff may sue for declaration agency action illegal or for injunction requiring/preventing official action; relief is equitable and discretionary.
entries.laymanExplanation: You ask court to say an agency acted unlawfully, order it to stop, or in proper cases require it to act.
entries.legalExplanation: Injunctions and declarations may be denied if public harms outweigh litigant's gains or remedy otherwise improper; mandatory injunction overlaps mandamus history.
entries.examApplication: Name specific requested order and whether judge has practical remedial discretion.
entries.examTrap: Even a legally correct plaintiff may not automatically receive every injunction requested.

entries.title: Mandatory versus prohibitory injunction
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: A prohibitory injunction stops action; mandatory injunction commands affirmative action; an affirmative demand can trigger mandamus-like restrictions.
entries.laymanExplanation: 'Don't do this' differs from 'you must do this.'
entries.legalExplanation: APA § 703 expressly authorizes both but courts sometimes examine whether command is a nondiscretionary legal duty.

entries.title: Mandamus under 28 U.S.C. § 1361
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: A writ compelling an officer generally requires a clear duty owed plaintiff, a ministerial/nondiscretionary act, no adequate alternative remedy, and relief remains extraordinary.
entries.laymanExplanation: You usually can't force an official to make a discretionary choice your way; you can demand that official do what law clearly requires.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal § 1361 authorizes district courts to issue mandamus; the Court's cases also look to exhaustion and indisputable entitlement.
entries.examApplication: Ask what text legally compels, whether discretion remains and whether an adequate ordinary APA remedy exists.
entries.examTrap: A statutory word 'may' alone seldom creates clear duty; disagreement over law is not automatically no clear duty.

entries.title: In re Cheney, 406 F.3d 723 (D.C. Cir. 2005)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: D.C. Circuit emphasized mandamus as drastic and extraordinary, reserved for clear and indisputable legal right.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tough remedy for uncommon cases.
entries.legalExplanation: Even a sufficiently supported petitioner does not receive writ as of right.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish § 1361 from ordinary § 1331 injunction.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Wolcott v. Sibelius, 635 F.3d 757 (5th Cir. 2011)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Doctor won ALJ Medicare payment decision but contractor withheld payment; clear ministerial duty and no alternate remedy warranted mandamus.
entries.laymanExplanation: If agency already had to pay and refused, court could compel payment.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts attempts to force open-ended policymaking.
entries.examApplication: Highlight clear legal entitlement.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Courts often prefer § 1331 injunctive remedies to mandamus
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Because mandamus has demanding prerequisites, counsel ordinarily seeks declaratory/injunctive relief through ordinary federal-question review; APA § 706(1) also authorizes compelling unlawfully withheld action.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not every effort to make government obey law needs the rare writ.
entries.legalExplanation: Check § 1331, APA § 702/703 and if inaction §§ 555(b), 706(1); substantive constraints still apply.
entries.examApplication: When a command is broad, compare SUWA's discrete legally required action rule.
entries.examTrap: Avoid thinking a 'mandatory injunction' makes § 706(1)'s limits disappear.

entries.title: Certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto, habeas
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Certiorari traditionally brings an inferior tribunal's record for review; prohibition prevents lower tribunal from proceeding without jurisdiction; quo warranto tests entitlement to office; habeas challenges unlawful confinement.
entries.laymanExplanation: These old writs serve specific problems but many modern federal challenges use declarations/injunctions.
entries.legalExplanation: Certiorari remains important for local adjudications in some states; habeas may cover certain alien/military custody and constitutional detention disputes.

entries.title: American School of Magnetic Healing v. McAnnulty, 187 U.S. 94 (1902)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court permitted injunction against unlawful Post Office mail-fraud exclusion even where older federal prerogative writs unavailable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Modern equitable remedies overcame historical writ limits.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency can be restrained from legally unsupported interference with mail.
entries.examApplication: Identify equitable relief where mandamus unavailable.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

topics.title: § 10.2 — Government Damages and Official Immunities (pp. 676–683; SKIM)
topics.description: Professor explicitly marks pp. 676–683 as skim. Concise issue-spotter only; not treated as fully assigned case law.

entries.title: SKIM: Federal Tort Claims Act baseline
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Under FTCA 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680, federal government has limited waiver of immunity for employee torts committed within employment analogous to private employer liability under state law.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sometimes the United States pays damages for its workers' negligence, but only within the law's exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: The FTCA contains exemptions for some intentional torts and discretionary functions; government liability is not the same as suits for injunction under APA § 702.
entries.examApplication: Flag whether claim is monetary FTCA tort versus administrative legality review.
entries.examTrap: Federal employees ordinarily not personally sued for employment-scope common-law torts due to Westfall substitution.

entries.title: SKIM: FTCA discretionary-function exception, Gaubert
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: § 2680(a) shields discretionary conduct susceptible to regulatory policy judgment, even if allegedly abusive; operational actions can qualify when policy-based.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government doesn't pay for every bad policy decision; ordinary careless driving is different.
entries.legalExplanation: Gaubert asks whether established policy permits judgment and whether challenged conduct is of kind grounded in policy analysis—not employee's subjective thoughts.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish actual policy judgment from mechanical violation of specific rule or careless vehicle operation.
entries.examTrap: Policy judgment exception is not unlimited immunity for any choice an employee makes.

entries.title: SKIM: State sovereign immunity versus local liability
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Eleventh Amendment/state sovereign immunity constrains private federal suits against states; local governments lack that immunity but § 1983 municipal liability requires policy/custom.
entries.laymanExplanation: Suing a state isn't the same as suing a city, and suing an official for future relief is different again.
entries.legalExplanation: Ex parte Young allows prospective federal-law injunction against state officer; Monell limits local liability to official policy/custom; some federal statutes under § 5 Fourteenth Amendment can abrogate state immunity.
entries.examApplication: Mention if hypothetical asks damages from state or municipal government.
entries.examTrap: Do not infer that all damages claims against state agencies are available because individual official acted wrongfully.

entries.title: SKIM: § 1983 versus limited Bivens claims
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: § 1983 provides federal constitutional/statutory-right claims against state/local officials; Bivens permits limited constitutional damages claims against federal officials, but Supreme Court resists extension.
entries.laymanExplanation: The way you sue state officials for constitutional damages isn't automatically available against federal ones.
entries.legalExplanation: Ziglar and Egbert refuse extension in new settings citing national security/alternative remedy/separation of powers; individual liability requires official involvement.
entries.examApplication: Identify government actor and specific cause of action.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim Bivens universally applies to every constitutional violation.

entries.title: SKIM: absolute and qualified immunity
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Butz granted absolute immunity to agency adjudicators/prosecutors in adjudicatory functions, qualified immunity to other officials, with violations of clearly established law generally needed for personal damages.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some officials can't be sued for specific adjudicative acts; others escape liability unless unlawfulness was clear.
entries.legalExplanation: Harlow objective standard; no vicarious personal liability (Iqbal); Westfall substitution for employee common-law torts; presidential civil immunity scope recognized.
entries.examApplication: Classify defendant and function, then examine clearly established right.
entries.examTrap: Do not mistake a governmental entity's immunity for an individual's, or constitutional damages for tort damages.

topics.title: § 10.2.3 — Presidential Criminal Immunity, Trump v. United States (pp. 683–685)
topics.description: Assigned detailed pp. 683–685: official/unofficial acts; absolute, presumptive and no immunity; majority, dissent and evidentiary implications. Opinion discussed by casebook, not fully excerpted.

entries.title: Trump v. United States, 603 U.S. 593 (2024) — official act immunity
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: The casebook distinguishes absolute immunity for core exclusive presidential constitutional acts, presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal charges against a President are treated differently depending on official versus private conduct.
entries.legalExplanation: Source sketches majority and Sotomayor dissent; this is background within predominantly skimmed segment and not a full assigned case opinion.
entries.examApplication: Separate criminal official-act doctrine from civil damages immunity.
entries.examTrap: Distinguish presidential criminal immunity from the separate civil damages immunity described earlier; official character must be analyzed without looking to subjective motive.
entries.sourceRole: Case described and briefly quoted in casebook discussion; full court opinion is not reproduced

entries.title: Absolute immunity: exclusive core constitutional functions
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: President is absolutely immune from federal criminal prosecution for conduct within exclusive, conclusive and preclusive presidential constitutional authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certain core presidential functions cannot serve as basis for criminal charges.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter identifies President–Justice Department official discussions as covered in Trump v United States; classification focuses constitutional source of power, not subjective motives.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether activity belongs to exclusive Article II sphere where Congress cannot regulate.
entries.examTrap: Do not extend this category to every action President undertakes.

entries.title: Presumptive immunity for remaining official acts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: For other official presidential conduct, at minimum a presumption against prosecution applies unless government shows no danger of intruding on presidential function.
entries.laymanExplanation: Other presidential work gets powerful but not necessarily absolute protection.
entries.legalExplanation: The opinion discussed Vice Presidential certification communications, state-election interactions and public statements as matters for lower-court classification; majority remanded for official-versus-unofficial assessment.
entries.examApplication: Identify official responsibility, shared constitutional powers, and whether government can rebut presumption.
entries.examTrap: An act's political controversy does not alone make it official or unofficial.

entries.title: Unofficial acts receive no presidential immunity
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Criminal conduct genuinely outside presidential official responsibilities does not receive immunity under Trump.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being President doesn't protect unrelated private conduct.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts must distinguish capacity in which President acted. Court may not investigate President's motives to label an act official or unofficial.
entries.examApplication: Analyze nature and authority of conduct and procedural proof limits.
entries.examTrap: Don't categorize acts merely because motive alleged improper.

entries.title: Evidence and motive restrictions
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: The casebook explains majority's ban on probing presidential motives to classify acts and its restriction on using immunized official-act evidence to prove criminal liability for unofficial acts.
entries.laymanExplanation: The rule affects not only which conduct can be charged, but what evidence prosecutors can use.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Barrett did not join majority's evidentiary exclusion reasoning; dissent criticized exclusion as obscuring mens rea for private wrongdoing.
entries.examApplication: Separate substantive official-act immunity from evidentiary limitation and identify Justice Barrett disagreement.
entries.examTrap: A discussion of criminal proof is not an automatic total immunity for every alleged act.

entries.title: Sotomayor dissent and constitutional arguments
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Justice Sotomayor criticized broad official-act criminal immunity as placing Presidents above law and disputed historical and textual basis, citing impeachment clauses and incentives for abuse.
entries.laymanExplanation: The dissent worries officials could misuse presidential power without criminal accountability.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority emphasized avoiding retaliatory prosecution across administrations, while dissent emphasized rule of law and constitutional accountability; disagreement is normative and constitutional, not two current rules.
entries.examApplication: Compare majority and dissent concisely; identify which governs.
entries.examTrap: Do not present dissent as holding.

topics.title: § 10.3 — Attorney Fees, American Rule, Lodestar and EAJA (pp. 685–690)
topics.description: Detailed assigned reading: fee awards, prevailing-party status, two EAJA statutes, substantial justification and Monroe problem.

entries.title: American rule: each side pays own attorney fees
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Absent statutory fee-shifting or an accepted limited exception, parties ordinarily bear their own attorneys' fees; 'private attorney general' benefit does not itself justify award.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning against government doesn't automatically make government pay your lawyer.
entries.legalExplanation: Alyeska Pipeline repudiated federal common-law public-interest exception; exceptions may include bad faith/common fund and specific statutes.
entries.examApplication: Find a governing fee statute before any lodestar calculation.
entries.examTrap: Strong public policy value alone does not override American rule in federal courts.

entries.title: Alyeska Pipeline Service Co. v. Wilderness Society, 421 U.S. 240 (1975)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Court rejected judicially invented private-attorney-general fee exception, leaving general fee-shifting choices to legislature.
entries.laymanExplanation: The group stopped pipeline work but couldn't claim fees just for doing public good.
entries.legalExplanation: American rule applies absent statute or recognized exception.
entries.examApplication: Contrast California statutory private-enforcement fee rule.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

entries.title: California private attorney general fee provision
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1021.5 authorizes fees for successful enforcement of important public rights, substantial public benefit and appropriate private-enforcement necessity/burden.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some states let public-interest litigation winners recover fees if the lawsuit vindicates rights of many people.
entries.legalExplanation: Apply California-specific statutory elements and necessity versus financial burden.
entries.examApplication: This is a state statute, not federal Alyeska exception.

entries.title: Lodestar computation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Reasonable fees generally equal reasonable hours reasonably spent times a reasonable hourly rate; 'fees on fees' may count.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calculate hours times the justified hourly rate—not necessarily the contract rate billed to client.
entries.legalExplanation: Perdue says enhancements above lodestar are rare; exceptional recovery delays might justify interest-based adjustment.
entries.examApplication: Write formula: reasonable hours × reasonable hourly rate; examine overhead, duplicative hours and reasonableness before product.
entries.examTrap: Don't automatically add 75% for quality of representation just because result was extraordinary.

entries.title: Perdue v. Kenny A., 559 U.S. 542 (2010)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court reversed a 75% fee enhancement over $6 million lodestar after very successful foster care litigation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even superb lawyers generally receive lodestar amount.
entries.legalExplanation: Objective fee predictability; limited delay-of-payment exceptional enhancement recognized.
entries.examApplication: Identify improper success-based bonus versus authorized interest-delay.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in chapter notes; full judicial opinion not reproduced

entries.title: EAJA administrative fee awards — 5 U.S.C. § 504
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Qualified prevailing party in Type A agency adjudication may recover attorney fees unless agency demonstrates its position substantially justified or special circumstances unjust; statutory exclusions apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: An eligible person who wins certain formal agency hearings may recover reasonable fees, but not in every hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: § 504 covers APA §§ 554,556,557 Type A where government represented by counsel; excludes rate-making or license applications; Type B/C not covered according to textbook.
entries.examApplication: Determine adjudication type, whether government counsel present, party eligible, winning party, exceptions.
entries.examTrap: Don't assume deportation adjudication is Type A; Ardestani rejected administrative EAJA in that setting.

entries.title: EAJA judicial fee awards — 28 U.S.C. § 2412(d)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Qualified prevailing party in non-tort civil action brought by/against U.S. can recover fees from judicial review of agency rules or adjudication, unless government substantially justified or other statutory bar.
entries.laymanExplanation: A person can qualify for fee recovery after winning judicial review even if administrative hearing wasn't a Type A case.
entries.legalExplanation: Judicial version can apply to rules and Types A, B, or C adjudications. Jurisdiction and favorable judicial result separately established.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether fees are from agency hearing (§ 504) or court challenge (§ 2412(d)).
entries.examTrap: Do not apply agency § 504's formal-hearing limitation to judicial § 2412(d).

entries.title: EAJA eligibility, statutory ceiling and historical figures
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Book reports eligibility thresholds: individual net worth ≤ $2m; business ≤ $7m plus ≤500 employees, with some nonprofit exemptions; $125/hour statutory cap indexed for inflation, cited as about $244/hour in 2023.
entries.laymanExplanation: EAJA mainly helps eligible individuals/smaller businesses and qualifying nonprofits; it has its own fee rate limitations.
entries.legalExplanation: Rate in source is 2023 historical and should not be represented as updated 2026 rate; adjustment sometimes permitted for specialist expertise and actual reasonable inflation increase.
entries.examApplication: Use threshold and rate in a textbook fact pattern, with explicit as-of-year qualification; check current values separately for real filing.
entries.examTrap: Never silently use market billing rate when EAJA cap applies; don't apply 2023 number as live current rate.

entries.title: Substantially justified = reasonable in law and fact
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Government has burden of showing its agency and litigation positions had reasonable legal and factual bases; losing the underlying case does not automatically mean government's position unjustified.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government can lose yet still reasonably have litigated the issue.
entries.legalExplanation: Pierce v. Underwood sets standard; Bricks v. EPA allowed government substantial justification despite inability to prove wetland hydrologic connection.
entries.examApplication: Separate litigation outcome from whether government's position was reasonable all along.
entries.examTrap: Do not infer fee award just because agency decision was vacated.

entries.title: Prevailing party and no catalyst-only recovery
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Fee awards ordinarily require judicial judgment on merits or court-approved consent decree materially changing legal relationship; voluntary policy change induced by suit usually insufficient.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting the government to back down may not count as officially winning for fee purposes.
entries.legalExplanation: Buckhannon rejected catalyst theory and can induce 'strategic capitulation' just before judgment; several fee statutes including EAJA apply this approach.
entries.examApplication: Check whether litigation produced enforceable judgment or consent decree versus voluntary mootness.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically treat settlement agreement without judicial imprimatur as fee-triggering judgment.

entries.title: Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia, 532 U.S. 598 (2001)

entries.summary: State changed challenged statute after suit; voluntary legislative change did not make plaintiff prevailing party.
entries.laymanExplanation: Causing a policy change doesn't equal winning court-ordered relief.

problems.title: Judicial review forum selection
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 670–672)
problems.prompt: Compare direct appellate review for a complex NRC rule, district-court review for large-volume Social Security claims, and state trial-court Article 78 review. How do statutory text, evidence-taking needs, costs and access shape correct forum?

problems.title: Jurisdiction versus APA waiver
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 672)
problems.prompt: An individual challenges federal agency action without an enabling-act review provision. Distinguish § 1331 jurisdiction, APA § 702 sovereign immunity waiver, § 703 form of action and § 706 scope of review.

problems.title: Mandamus versus ordinary equitable relief
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 673–675)
problems.prompt: Agency refuses to act on a mandatory license issuance; alternatively agency refuses to change discretionary licensing policy. Contrast mandamus, declaration, injunction and § 706(1) limits without deciding a new fact pattern.

problems.title: Mercury Stores / Commission pornography-boycott report — SKIM
problems.kind: Textbook problem in skim reading — UNSOLVED
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 683)
problems.prompt: Commission appointed by President or state governor criticizes non-obscene erotic magazines, names retailers selling Penthouse, and urges private boycotts. Mercury suffers picketing losses. Analyze damages against government versus individual commissioners, common-law/constitutional theories, § 1983/Bivens, immunity, and First Amendment without solving.

problems.title: Monroe Mary & Bernice housing-discrimination fee hypothetical
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 690)
problems.prompt: Monroe enacted EAJA-like statute and California § 1021.5 analogue. Mary and Bernice sued landlord Ruth for sexual-orientation discrimination. Commission rejected case on fact and statutory coverage, reviewing court sustained factual finding but corrected the statute's sexual-orientation coverage. Agency litigation fees: 60 hours × $400; court review fees: 40 hours × $400; fees paid by tax-exempt advocacy organization. Determine eligibility, prevailing-party status, substantial justification, fee caps, public interest and how much of either claim agency may be compelled to pay. Leave all calculations and conclusion unsolved.

problems.title: Fee-shifting: when recovery is allowed
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 686–690)
problems.prompt: Compare Alyeska federal default, California public-interest fee statute, § 504 administrative EAJA and § 2412(d) judicial EAJA, and whether a voluntary government concession after suit creates prevailing-party status.

problems.title: EAJA calculation drill — no solutions
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 670–690 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 687–689)
problems.prompt: In a hypothetical qualifying case, test lodestar, maximum statutory hourly cap, inflation adjustment (using historical year values supplied in question), net-worth criteria, expert costs and whether government was substantially justified. Write formulas but leave outcome unanswered.
